locator.heading: Balm

source_text:
THIS herb is so well known to be an inhabitant almost in every garden,
that I shall not need to write any discription thereof, although its
virtues, which are many, may not be omitted.

_Government and virtues._] It is an herb of Jupiter, and under Cancer,
and strengthens nature much in all its actions. Let a syrup made with
the juice of it and sugar (as you shall be taught at the latter end of
this book) be kept in every gentlewoman’s house to relieve the weak
stomachs and sick bodies of their poor sickly neighbours; as also the
herb kept dry in the house, that so with other convenient simples, you
may make it into an electuary with honey, according as the disease
is you shall be taught at the latter end of my book. The Arabian
physicians have extolled the virtues thereof to the skies; although the
Greeks thought it not worth mentioning. Seraphio says, it causes the
mind and heart to become merry, and revives the heart, faintings and
swoonings, especially of such who are overtaken in sleep, and drives
away all troublesome cares and thoughts out of the mind, arising from
melancholy or black choler; which Avicen also confirms. It is very good
to help digestion, and open obstructions of the brain, and hath so
much purging quality in it (saith Avicen) as to expel those melancholy
vapours from the spirits and blood which are in the heart and arteries,
although it cannot do so in other parts of the body. Dioscorides says,
that the leaves steeped in wine, and the wine drank, and the leaves
externally applied, is a remedy against the stings of a scorpion, and
the bitings of mad dogs; and commends the decoction thereof for women
to bathe or sit in to procure their courses; it is good to wash aching
teeth therewith, and profitable for those that have the bloody flux.
The leaves also, with a little nitre taken in drink, are good against
the surfeit of mushrooms, helps the griping pains of the belly; and
being made into an electuary, it is good for them that cannot fetch
their breath: Used with salt, it takes away wens, kernels, or hard
swelling in the flesh or throat; it cleanses foul sores, and eases
pains of the gout. It is good for the liver and spleen. A tansy or
caudle made with eggs, and juice thereof while it is young, putting to
it some sugar and rose-water, is good for a woman in child-birth, when
the after-birth is not thoroughly voided, and for their faintings upon
or in their sore travail. The herb bruised and boiled in a little wine
and oil, and laid warm on a boil, will ripen it, and break it.

ema_monograph.title: Melissae folium (melissa/lemon balm)
ema_monograph.relevance_note: Confirms traditional use for nervous tension and digestive complaints, noting lack of evidence for gynecological fluxes or bleeding.

pubmed.title: The effects of lemon balm (Melissa officinalis L.) on depression and anxiety in clinical trials: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pubmed.relevance_note: Reviews efficacy for anxiety/depression, not historical uses like quartan agues or fluxes.

pubmed.title: Melissa officinalis L. - A review of its traditional uses, phytochemistry and pharmacology.
pubmed.relevance_note: Discusses historical applications for nervous disorders and digestion, contrasting with older gynecological uses.

pubmed.title: Clinical Efficacy and Tolerability of Lemon Balm (Melissa officinalis L.) in Psychological Well-Being: A Review.
pubmed.relevance_note: Focuses on modern psychological well-being, offering no data on traditional uses like vomiting or quartan agues.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence supports Melissa officinalis for anxiety and digestive issues. Historical uses for 'fluxes,' 'bleedings,' or 'quartan agues' lack contemporary clinical validation, though the plant's calming effects on vomiting may align with modern anti-nausea findings.

pubmed.title: RETRACTED: Neuroprotective Effects of Dried Tubers of Aconitum napellus.
pubmed.relevance_note: Retracted study on neuroprotection, potentially relevant to 'falling-sickness' but lacks safety data.

pubmed.title: Protective effects of the exogenous application of salicylic acid and chitosan on chromium-induced photosynthetic capacity and osmotic adjustment in Aconitum napellus.
pubmed.relevance_note: Study on plant physiology, not human therapeutic use for skin or systemic conditions.

pubmed.title: Antidiabetic activity of standardized dried tubers extract of Aconitum napellus in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats.
pubmed.relevance_note: Demonstrates antidiabetic effects in rats, unrelated to traditional uses for vertigo or skin.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence highlights neuroprotective and antidiabetic properties but does not support traditional claims for vertigo or skin spots. Crucially, the species contains potent cardiotoxic alkaloids; modern research emphasizes severe toxicity rather than therapeutic efficacy for these specific ailments.

concordance.rationale: Melissa officinalis shows clinical support for anxiety/depression (PMID:34449930), partially aligning with 'melancholy' claims. Aconitum napellus is toxic; evidence contradicts safety for internal use against 'weak stomachs' or 'bitings'.
concordance.uncertainty: Historical 'scorpion' and 'dog bite' claims lack specific modern efficacy data for these taxa.
caveats: Aconitum is highly toxic; internal use is unsafe.
Historical 'melancholy' maps to modern anxiety, not historical humoral theory.

issues: Unearned Grade: The entry assigns a 'B' grade with 'partial' direction. However, the evidence explicitly states that Aconitum napellus is toxic and contradicts safety claims for internal use ('weak stomachs', 'bitings'). Assigning a positive or even partially positive concordance grade to a toxic plant used for internal ailments without qualifying the grade as 'Fail' or 'Contraindicated' constitutes an unearned grade. The rationale admits contradiction but fails to reflect this in the final grade.

Missing Evidence: Claims regarding 'scorpion' and 'dog bite' treatments lack specific modern efficacy data, yet these are treated as part of the entry's scope without a clear resolution or negative evidence flagging them as unsupported.
